text: You approved the last plan with all 3 quick checks wrong.
A quick check is the video's question on what the plan will do.
The second one used 4 words the video never explained.
A call is a choice the agent makes on its own,
outside the plan.
A tag says why you might look at a call:
visible, hard to undo, or close,
meaning either way is reasonable.
A streak counts calls with one tag accepted in a row;
at 10, they stop pausing the video.
A miss is something a review let through,
fixed later.
Without them, the check can't be read.
Some fixes are built separately, not asked here.
A card before each video lists its prerequisites,
the videos to watch first; by default,
the system video, which explains the whole tool.
A panel lists the video's words.
No decision is named by its number alone.
A wrong answer can be walked through.
Approving notes missed checks.
The build flags unexplained words.
4 steps go deeper.
One: every word explained once, one click away.
2: the tool picks what to watch first.
3: it remembers where you got lost.
4: checks test the main idea.
Step 2 needs step 1; 3 and 4 stand alone.
Step 1.
The glossary is the repo's list of words,
one meaning each.
Each gets a beat of the system video that explains it;
a beat is one short scene.
No beat explains a streak yet,
so the system video's build stops and names it.
And clicking a word in the captions shows its meaning.
Quick check.
The glossary has streak, and no beat of the system video explains it.
What happens when the system video is built?
Question one: which words should you see?
A: plain ones, like choice for call and label for tag;
the files keep theirs.
B: today's words, each explained.
I recommend A: a word that says what it means needs no explaining.
Which one?
With A, you see choice and label;
the files still say call and tag.
With B, you see call and tag,
and each is explained.
Step 2.
Today, prerequisites are guessed; now the tool picks them:
the system video, plus up to 2 videos of plans this one builds on.
The last plan builds on the streak of 10,
decided in the revise-loop plan, so its card lists the system video,
then the revise-loop video.
Quick check.
The last plan builds on the streak of 10,
decided in the revise-loop plan.
Which videos does its card list?
Question 2: the card ticks what you've watched.
Where is that kept?
A: this browser at once, and your own file,
read by every repo, once you send a review.
B: only the reviews you send.
I recommend A: the card needs it at once,
the tool in every repo.
Which one?
With A, a finished video is ticked at once,
and in every repo once sent.
With B, a video counts as watched once you send its review.
Step 3.
Memory is what the tool learns from your reviews.
It gains a line for getting lost:
checks wrong, explanations opened, words looked up,
approvals with checks missed.
A word looked up in 3 reviews gets its beat marked for a rewrite.
Quick check.
You look up streak in 3 reviews.
What happens?
Question 3: can approving be blocked when you answered checks wrong?
A: never; the review records approved with 3 of 3 missed.
B: blocked when all were missed,
until you open each explanation.
I recommend A: a record fixes the next video;
a block just teaches clicking through.
Which one?
With A, you can always approve,
and the record shows what you missed.
With B, 3 of 3 missed means 3 explanations before approving.
Step 4.
A quick check tests its beat's main idea,
on the case the beat just showed,
with nothing new.
The last plan's first check asked about an exception said in passing;
its beat showed 8 pauses becoming one.
Now the check asks about those 8.
The build warns when an answer isn't in its beat.
Quick check.
A beat shows 8 pauses in one step becoming one.
Which check follows step 4?
That's the plan: every word explained once,
prerequisites the tool picks, a memory of where you got lost,
and checks on the main idea.
Draw on a step to leave a note,
or approve.
Narration and visuals are AI-generated.
